paragraphs: In short, my setup as of today is this:
2x GPT PRO MAX ($400)
3x Kimi PRO MAX ($600)
4x Qwen PRO MAX ($272)
GPT 5.6 Sol Max — the smartest
Kimi K3 Max — the balanced one
Qwen3.8max — the most talented
But
GPT is the most throttled in both directions:
1) There's a great deal it's not allowed to do, and believe me, everything it's not allowed affects absolutely everything it does, including what it is allowed.

2) Each next step up in reasoning doesn't just make it smarter but again FORBIDS IT TO BE DUMBER. Hence the manic-ness and the hours/days where it could have coped perfectly in minutes. Hundreds of files where a piece of one would have been enough, etc.

And this looping from point 2 isn't baked into the model, but is a side effect that worsens during work. The deeper into the woods, the fatter these wolves. So any reasoning levels above Medium should be used only to think with, but you can work with them only on a sufficiently narrow/simple task in which the model simply won't have time to go insane and do more harm than good.

In the end it turned out that GPT 5.6 Sol MEDIUM is essentially the same GPT 5.5 xhigh, only smarter thanks to the properties the model has independent of reasoning. For example, 5.6's eyes are set much farther apart than 5.5's, and thanks to that it sees the parts of a task 5.5 doesn't.
In short, I lost all interest in using 5.5 once I figured out 5.6.

Our brethren were simply caught by their own greed. A person from the Russian provinces just can't believe that the badge reading “almost the top … for worthless scum” is exactly what he needs. Such a person will buy any ABIBAS if the price tag says “LUXE”…
It's also important that in the config the thinking effort for plan mode is configured separately, and that one you can indeed set to Max/Ultra.

As a result I run all tasks through plan mode. 5.6 Sol Max, with its manic gaze, hunts down every speck of dust and makes a plan at a level I think in places exceeding the capabilities of GPT 5.5 PRO, while the implementation of that plan goes to 5.6 Sol Medium, which is smart enough to simply write all the needed code flawlessly and do all the needed work by hand.
KIMI

I fairly quickly understood that Kimi is a great model, but I also quickly understood that it can't hold a candle to GPT 5.6 in terms of intelligence. Kimi is the winner of the 5.5 lineup (and even then, on precision of result in terms of the number of generated bugs or completely missed important zones, I'd argue), but not 5.6. Not even close.

However, KIMI is an absolutely unsurpassed designer. I draw designs with it simply on kimi.ai, the websites button. I liked drawing with Claude Design, but it probably says something that not once since I opened Kimi Design have I missed Claude Design, and I haven't gone in there even though I have an Anthropic subscription too; I simply no longer count that family in the roster, it's purely a nice-to-have for experiments and testing new things that'll come out there.

Kimi is also useful for throwing long Codex sessions at it (basically almost any of my sessions last 15-30-50 hours) and asking about progress and an alternative opinion on what's happening in the session. Throwing in sessions is simply right-click … the mouse on the session ID in the GPT APP, paste into Kimi and say, yo sis, please look at how events are developing there and tell me what you think.
That's a useful motion that saves time, reduces stress, lets you think a little more perceptively ahead. And sometimes gives real grounds for invading a Codex session with some thunderous steer.

Having Kimi itself code, making its own decisions about what to code, why and how — I've practically stopped. If GPT is running low on resources, it's the moment to have Codex stop coding with its own hands and manage Kimi's coding sessions.

It's not ideal, because at some point I accumulated enough observations to say with confidence: models manage each other very … poorly. However, if there are … excess limits on Kimi, then even if the development efficiency of GPT Sol -> Kimi drops severalfold, it's more tolerable than milking Codex to zero so as to then … bugs with Kimi and then fix them with Codex =)))))) … I've had it with that.

Qwen3.8max, by the way, was gorgeous hands for Codex, but sailed off, because its speed was slowed roughly 50 times and the token cost suspiciously approached the API token cost. Thus Qwen became simply the most expensive thing in nature if used for development, by far.

However, Qwen3.8max is the most talented writer, capable of writing BETTER THAN MOST PEOPLE. At least in the hands of someone who can also write reasonably well. And the ability to write that well can't exist on its own. It's simply superbly prepared in any humanities matter, and you can't call that useless in any way.

That means it's a wonderful companion to 5.6 Sol and Kimi for some important protracted brainstorms, a judge of everything related to the emission of any words anywhere by any model, a formulator of contracts and principles for other models, etc. The longer I practice with it, the more and better I understand how and why to use it in the small things.
Qwen also has all sorts of fancy models in its CLI, like GLM and others, which you can pull and not envy that someone has a cat-wife and you don't.
Mythos sucks.
And of course don't forget that any model is at MOST 50% of the influence on the result.

The other 50% is your own harness (Agents.md and the rest of the matryoshka of logical contracts the LLMs will execute every session or when addressing specific repos), your skill (I learned a lot last week, which means I couldn't do it before, even though I've been vibe-coding since last September), your nervous system, stamina, etc. etc.

The more I talk with different people one-on-one about vibe-coding, the more I understand that the gap between me and them is growing, because I keep sitting ALL DAY, while they don't sit down even every day and don't spend more than a few hours in the process.
Listening to them, I understand that throwing advice over my shoulder won't bring them any benefit, just as I once understood about consulting..

Hmm, over the past couple of months I've spent all my blood down to the last drop, as well as all the blood of every other resident of San Francisco, to arrive at the point with my long-suffering repo where I've arrived.

And so, before launch, essentially all I have left is to finish the design of some client-facing systems, because in the ones I'd knocked together in a hurry even I got lost, which means a person who hadn't been building this system all these long months would have had no chance at all :DDD
Historically Codex and GPT inside it did design very crappily. So crappily that I sort of stopped trying.
Since March (or whenever Claude Design was released?) I cranked out designs with Anthropic. That's basically the only thing the models there are fit for on a subscription.

Last week I got a taste for Kimi. Largely, of course, having fallen for the marketing benchmarks claiming Kimi is 30% cooler than Fable in design, which in turn is cooler than everyone else on the market.
Kimi made good design, I liked it. Can't say it's gorgeous. And I didn't see the 30% difference from Fable either. Just tidy design. No worse, and thanks for that)

My attitude toward Codex on design was also, of course, undermined by our discussion chat, where nobody ever once sang serenades to GPT the designer, yet every other day someone loudly kicked it in the … over design.
I believe the chat, since who else to believe; I sort of have no other true nerds of this business of ours in my surroundings =(((
And then Ox Alpha appeared, and people started saying, like, it draws design a lot … than Kimi.

Today my Codex, with the 5.6 Sol Max model, spent a good 10 hours re-mangling the product from the old UI Frankenstein consisting of frameworks randomly stuck in at different times and in places plain bare HTML/CSS onto the combination React + Tailwind CSS 4 + shadcn approach + Base UI + our own SLSBMB Design System.

That combination was born after I ran, on six different models + GPT PRO, the task of studying my project under a magnifying glass, thoroughly understanding the different levels of this project's logic and estimating which UI technology set would suit us best given that 100% of the effort to develop and configure all this crap was and will continue to be done exclusively by LLMs, and we want to stop living in visual chaos and unpredictability and start living in a world of a thought-through, calibrated, researched, meaningful visual system.

In the end each of the models proposed different combinations, laying out strengths and weaknesses, but 10 out of 10 ranked precisely this combination highest on every point. Without colluding, with genuinely 97% overlap. The only place they diverged twice was Regex vs Base UI.
I immediately googled that the shadcn crowd dropped Regex in favor of Base UI this summer, decided it was a sign, and glassed in my choice.

So the brand-new front end is implemented, and it's time to work on the missing design upgrades, but who to do them with I somehow couldn't figure out. In the end I went to Codex and asked it to make one big fat edit on one of the sets of screens most important to me with four mutually independent sessions at once: GPT 5.6 Sol Medium, Opus 5 max, Kimi K3 max, Ox Alpha max.
And who'd have thought — Ox Alpha handled the task worst of all.
And best of all… GPT 5.6 Sol Medium!?!?!?!
I tried once more — and again GPT 5.6 Sol Medium beat everyone by a wide margin.

And everything about it was better than the others'. The colors, and the understanding of why the screens are needed and what ailments each has, what problem we're solving for the people who use them, the pixel precision of all the paddings, fonts, etc. (here Ox Alpha is especially bad; it works on the scheme “text landed in the box — that's already a … victory,” at best at Qwen3.8's level).

A little question for the chat: why does nobody praise Sol on design?!?! Have you, like me, simply not tried it in a long time, or is it the magic set React + Tailwind CSS 4 + shadcn approach + Base UI + our own SLSBMB Design System that worked like that?

GPT, by the way, said I'd been quite underestimating all along the correct choice of technologies for the front end, and that's a common problem on the market. Some people choose “fashionable” frameworks on which the model produces less than 30% accuracy, whereas on the neighboring one, on which it was trained especially well, it's long been minting a hundred. Maybe that's what I'm observing? =)
But that alone doesn't explain why, on this same set, all the others flopped so hard.

Given that Codex has its own most convenient design tool built right into Codex, the best image generator, a gorgeous understanding of animations and special effects, it saddened me greatly that it designed worse. If that's been fixed, then one (big) headache fewer. And Kimi in that case is no longer needed even for the collection. Qwen3.8 writes texts better, and GPT does everything else better. And 5.6 Sol Medium runs inference faster (severalfold, and severalfold cheaper in token leakage at this reasoning level). So there's no work left for Kimi at all =(

So now many people continue to praise or even worship Kimi
But they're most likely doing something like one thing

To everyone who falls for the posts of four-eyes on Odnoklassniki and LinkedIn who saw an ad for the new Mac mini and fancied themselves a data center once they save up to buy this hardware of the future on credit:

Right now I'm very nerdily running an interview feature whose job is to extract the needed info from a client while carefully entertaining him, and then write a correctly structured article from which pieces will fly off into JSONs for other tasks.

So the model has to chat and at the end make sense of the whole chat, run its meanings through deterministic doctrines, get a non-deterministic intellectual result out of it, dodge prompt injections and people who want to sell dismembered bodies and other dark stuff of various kinds, but at the same time not kill anyone who wants to sell gray-area stuff.
Sounds increasingly complex somehow, but even the previously mentioned 4o could have handled that.

I asked 5.6 Sol Max, Kimi K3 and qwen3.8-max to run tests in parallel, and their task is to take all the models on the market, bottom-up (from dumb to smart), and run 100 tasks on each, to understand capabilities, stability, and determine the finalists on which we'll then run separate experiments.

Budget for the whole experiment ~$800. But quality in this spot is very important to me, so I'll pour in much more if I have to) Before this, Qwen3.8-max low and 5.6 Sol Low had checked in there, but didn't justify themselves, each for its own reasons, and now I understand that I'll have to build a layer cake of models there for it to work the way I need.
So: the experiment has been going for a long time, and now it's reached GLM 5 and Qwen3-max.
Even in the cloud these models show results so far below the specified minimum baseline that their activity can basically be neglected. Absolutely useless crap.

I understand why such models might be needed in factory conditions. I once had a friend who did elementary machine-learning automation like “photograph the chicken, use machine vision to determine whether there's cellophane on it, if yes — the light blinks once, if no — twice.”
That's why they exist.
But I can hardly imagine people with such tasks sitting in a Telegram chat and being able to read or discuss this at all.

And everyone sitting in Telegram reading/discussing how they'll run some unlimited Qwen 27b to the death of the capitalists on a thousand-dollar piece of crap (and a Mac mini beats up the wallet pretty well by the way; in a decent config it costs about four thousand?!) — expose themselves as theorists, and this is sci-fi at the level of “Thomas the Tank Engine.”
How to do design and UI if you understand nothing about it at all

Yesterday I wrote a post about the suffering caused by having to take responsibility not only for the code but for the design too. And for me that's a problem. Because when you vibe-code a solution, at first you can set aside existential things like code cleanliness, security, bugs, and orient by the result — does it work or not.

But when it comes to visuals and usability, the nuances begin. The first thing AI gives you for the request “create a website” is a blue-violet gradient, the Inter font and a typical landing-page skeleton.

By the way, this AI slop of websites is the fault of the popular CSS framework Tailwind; back in 2019 they made indigo the default color of buttons in their components, the tutorials spread across all of GitHub, and the models learned that median.

Tailwind's creator Adam Wathan later publicly admitted he chose indigo not for design reasons but as a neutral placeholder for demos. And that shade of lavender has already been nicknamed “VibeCode Purple.”

And then the circulation of AI slop in the nature of web design begins. Vibe-coded sites get onto the web, the next generation of models already learns from them, the average self-reinforces. Plus the agent additionally narrows the choice to what's easier to lay out.
So how do you break this purple circle if you have no designer's eye? Here's what I fed my agent and myself:

— ui-skills.com — a catalog of design-engineering skills for agents. Inside are skills from shadcn, Anthropic, Emil Kowalski and others. Plug in via CLI or MCP, and the agent starts laying out by the rules rather than by its own generic habits
— ui.shadcn.com — the industry standard, the foundation of the design systems of half the modern web. The component code goes right into your project, so agents edit it freely and know this library better than any other. Free
— coss.com/ui — a fresh library of a pile of components on top of Base UI, tuned among other things for AI applications. Open source
— designsystemchecklist.com — a checklist. A list of what must be covered in a design system, from colors to documentation. Feed it to the agent as a quality frame against which it checks your front end
— beautifului.dev — a component library specifically for AI interfaces. Chats, streaming loaders, code blocks, agent-action confirmation cards, workflow visualization. Copy and paste. Free
— beui.dev — animated components for React and Next.js on Framer Motion and Tailwind. Modals, buttons, tabs, toasts, docs. Installs via the shadcn CLI. Base is open source, there's a paid Pro
— rareui.com — a small collection of fun animated React components. Folders, letter gravity, liquid ball. Each component is one file, installed with one command. Completely free
— transitions.dev — a catalog of ready-made transitions and micro-animations. Modal opening, skeletons, number animation, card resizing. Copy the code or plug it into the agent as a separate skill. Base is free, the rest in Pro
— emilkowal.ski/ui/you-dont-need-animations — an essay by Emil Kowalski (author of the sonner and vaul libraries) on when animations hurt. For example, that frequent actions are better not animated and everything should stay faster than 300 ms. Feed it to the agent so it doesn't turn the interface into a cartoon
In short, during the vacation I didn't vibe-code anything at all, not once, didn't even look at the computer, and didn't think about my project for a minute… since last … Thursday.
Today Tuesday ended and Wednesday began. So… five days have passed? Six? I always had … with math, to the point of being kicked out of school.

All these days I caught and held focus with all my might on the road, on the hares, deer, sheep, lakes, larches and the greening, so sweet newborn needles at the tips of their … fluffy flexible little branches.

Galloping through all this natural idyll is fun of course, …, I love turning the wheel and I love Scotland, but it turns out I was getting so tired not from vibe-coding but from having lived another day as an already 38-year-old mortal carcass.
And I don't hate vibe-coding all that much; what troubles the head is rather that I haven't finished my project yet, on which absolutely everything is staked.
And not because I'm missing out on the worldly: there's … to miss out on.
In short, as usual I got tired of “resting” on the third day, and today is something like the sixth.

But a plan is a plan; tomorrow two days in Edinburgh, then another night in York, where I've never been, and at about four San Francisco time I'll walk into my sweet little office at home. Wait a little longer, buddy, I'm bringing whiskey!!!
I thought home on the third, but turns out it's the fifth; hanging in there.

About the new Fable I … absolutely, they're … as usual; I've already understood that Anthropic is a passed stage of AI until they change the CEO. But if OpenAI releases Astra this week, it'll be especially hard for me :D
Although as Sol's practice shows, it's surely most rational to start trying to use Astra in ~a month =)
Releasing a model that can work for days and weeks but won't work autonomously for even an hour)
Actually Sol can already work for days and weeks, and even GPT 5.5 since the goal era)
But if it gets rid of Sol's problems and gets much smarter in everything else — still …

I'll have to bother building a clicker for the “approve” button, if I understand correctly that that's how the mechanics will be, of course) Or we'll live at the computer; either way it won't last longer than a month until the next events)
